Fort Magrad- The southernmost bite of stone in Gloriano, a fortress planted in tundra so flat and merciless it makes the sky feel heavier. From a distance it looks like a dark blister on a white world; low, thick walls crouched against the wind, watchtowers rising like broken teeth, banners snapping stiff as boards.
The land around it is all hard silence: black rock ribs pushing through snowpack, ice-grass that cuts gloves when you grab it, and endless horizons that vanish the moment a storm decides to erase them. In that emptiness, Magrad doesn’t just stand out it dominates. It’s the only shape the tundra agrees to keep.
What makes Magrad different, what makes it possible is what it’s built on.
The fort sits directly atop a thermal geyser, a living wound in the earth that breathes heat into a country that wants everything frozen and dead. The builders anchored the foundation around a reinforced vent-chamber and carved channels through the bedrock, turning the geyser’s steam and warmth into a circulatory system. So while the tundra howls outside at killing temperatures, Magrad’s stone holds a secret summer in its bones.
You feel it the moment you cross the gate.
The walls are still brutal and practical basalt and iron-granite stacked thick, angled to shed wind and deflect siege but they’re faintly warm to the touch in sheltered places. The main corridors are laid over heated conduits, so the cold never fully claims the floors. In the deepest winters, when snow piles up like a second wall against the outer face, the fort’s interior stays livable: not comfortable, not soft just survivable, which is its own kind of luxury at the end of the world.
Serves as the command post for the Knighthood of the Blessed Dawn, led by Sir Niall.

Ulara- Set in the Death Frontier—a scar of ruined ground where the wind carries ash instead of salt and the horizon is always the wrong color—Ulara looks impossible at first sight. The land around it is dead country: petrified tree-stumps like broken ribs, gray dunes that swallow footprints overnight, and patches of glassy earth that ring under a boot as if the world were hollow there. In that wasteland, Ulara rises like a held breath.
The city itself is Wingly-built, but not Wingly-arrogant. Its architecture favors smooth, pale stone and weightless lines—arches that seem too thin to hold anything, balconies that jut like feathers, and bridges that curve with a calm elegance as if violence were an uncouth language spoken elsewhere. A faint shimmer often clings to its edges, not as a dramatic barrier, but as a practical one: a membrane of old craft that turns abrasive dust-storms and toxic gusts into harmless eddies. When the Frontier howls, Ulara does not flinch—it simply redirects the wind and continues its day.
At the center of the city is the Neutral Spire, a tall, narrow tower wrapped in wind-chimes and silvered vanes that never stop moving. It’s the city’s signal: a visible pledge that Ulara is open to all who come in peace—and an unspoken reminder that every arrival is being watched, measured, and recorded. Lanterns along the Spire burn in cool, steady hues at night, casting the city in the soft glow of a sea seen through ice.
Ulara’s streets are clean in a way that feels intentional rather than wealthy. Everything is designed for containment: covered thoroughfares to keep Frontier grit out of lungs, drainage channels etched with runes to rinse away tainted rain, and public courtyards dotted with low, warm vents where travelers thaw out and stop shaking long enough to speak without biting their tongues. There’s always the faint scent of mineral water and crushed herbs—Wingly antiseptics used like routine manners.
Neutrality here isn’t just a political stance. It’s the city’s entire economy.
